questions.prompt: What time does your working or studying day usually start?

segments.text: My day usually starts at half past eight, when I get to the office.
I get up at seven, have a quick breakfast and take the bus.
On Mondays I'm often a bit earlier, for example, because we have a team meeting at eight. I prefer starting early, because I can finish before it gets dark.
I'm at my desk by half past eight, more or less on the dot.
That means getting up at seven, grabbing a quick bite and catching the bus before the rush hour gets going.
Mondays are the exception, as we have a team meeting at eight. Still, I don't mind early starts, because I'm at my best in the morning.

questions.prompt: What do you like most about your job or your studies?

segments.text: What I like most is the people. My colleagues are friendly and always ready to help.
I also enjoy the variety, because every day is a bit different.
For example, yesterday I spent the morning on a report and the afternoon talking to customers. It never gets boring, and I always learn something new.
What I like most about my job is the people I work with. We get on really well, and there's a real sense of teamwork.
On top of that, no two days are the same, which keeps me on my toes.
One minute I'm buried in a report, the next I'm dealing with a customer, so I'm never bored.

questions.prompt: Would you like to be doing the same thing in five years' time?

segments.text: I'm not sure. I like my job, but I'd like to learn more and have more responsibility.
In five years, I hope to be a team leader or maybe a manager.
For example, I'm taking an evening course in management at the moment. If I don't get a promotion, I might look for a different company.
Probably not, to be honest. I'm happy where I am, but I wouldn't want to be stuck in a rut.
In five years' time, I'd like to be managing a small team, or perhaps even running my own business.
I've been taking evening classes in management, so I'm keeping my options open and we'll see what comes up.

questions.prompt: What do you study, or what did you study?

segments.text: I'm studying English at the moment, in an evening class twice a week.
Before that, I studied business at university, so I know a lot about marketing.
I decided to improve my English because I need it for my job. For example, I often have to write emails and join video calls with clients abroad.
At the moment I'm brushing up my English in an evening class, but my degree was in business administration.
I took the language course because it's become essential at work: emails, video calls, the lot.
I'd like to be able to hold my own in any meeting, which is why I've been practising every single day.

questions.prompt: How do you usually prepare for a test or an exam?

segments.text: I usually start preparing about three weeks before the exam.
First I make a study plan, and then I read my notes and do practice exercises every day.
For example, before my last English test I did one listening exercise each morning and wrote a short text at the weekend. I also try to sleep well the night before.
I like to plan well ahead, so I draw up a timetable about three weeks before the big day.
Then I work my way through my notes and do as many practice tests as I can.
The night before, I take it easy and get a proper night's sleep, since cramming at the last minute never works for me.

questions.prompt: Would you like to learn something new next year?

segments.text: Yes, I'd like to learn to play the guitar.
I've always loved music, but I've never had time to take lessons.
Next year I'll have more free time, so I'm planning to join a class near my house. I'd like to play a few songs for my friends by the end of the year.
I'd love to. I've always wanted to learn the guitar, but I've never got round to it.
Next year, I'm hoping to sign up for lessons once things calm down at work.
If I stick with it, I might even be able to play a couple of songs at a family party by December, which would be a real feather in my cap.

questions.prompt: How do you usually get to work or to your classes?

segments.text: I usually go by metro. It takes about twenty-five minutes.
I don't have a car, and the metro is faster than the bus, especially in the morning.
For example, if I take the bus, it can take almost an hour because of the traffic. I read or listen to music during the journey, so the time passes quickly.
I tend to take the metro, which gets me there in about twenty-five minutes door to door.
It beats the bus hands down, as you're not stuck in traffic.
I make the most of the journey by catching up on podcasts, so it doesn't feel like wasted time.

questions.prompt: What is public transport like where you live?

segments.text: It's quite good, I think. We have a metro, buses and a tram.
The trains are frequent and usually on time, and tickets aren't very expensive.
The only problem is at rush hour, when the metro is really crowded. For example, I often have to stand for the whole journey, but it's still better than driving.
On the whole, it's pretty reliable. There's an extensive metro network, plus buses and trams, and they run frequently.
Fares are reasonable, too, especially with a monthly pass.
The downside is that it's packed to the rafters at rush hour, but that's the price you pay for living in a big city.

questions.prompt: Would you prefer to live closer to your work or your place of study?

segments.text: Yes, I would. At the moment I spend almost an hour travelling every day.
If I lived closer, I'd have more free time and I wouldn't be so tired.
For example, I could walk or cycle, which is better for my health. However, rents are higher near the centre, so it's not easy.
Absolutely. I'm losing the best part of an hour each day on the commute, and it adds up.
If I lived within walking distance, I'd have more time for myself and I'd be getting some exercise into the bargain.
The catch is that rents near the centre are through the roof, so it's a trade-off I haven't been able to make.

questions.prompt: Where do you usually do your food shopping?

segments.text: I usually go to the supermarket near my house once a week.
It's convenient and it has a good choice of products at reasonable prices.
For example, I always buy fruit and vegetables at the local market on Saturdays, because they're fresher and cheaper. I do the rest of the shopping at the supermarket.
I do the bulk of my shopping at the supermarket round the corner, once a week.
But I'm quite particular about fruit and veg, so I pick those up at the local market on Saturdays.
The produce is fresher and, believe it or not, often cheaper, and I like having a chat with the stallholders.

questions.prompt: Do you enjoy shopping for clothes?

segments.text: Not really. I find it tiring, and the shops are always crowded.
I prefer buying only what I need, so I usually go once or twice a year.
For example, last month I needed a coat for the winter, so I spent one afternoon in the shopping centre and found one quickly. After that, I went straight home.
To be honest, it isn't my cup of tea. The shops are heaving, and I can never find my size.
I'm more of a get-in, get-out shopper: I make a list and stick to it.
Last winter, I bought a coat in under an hour, which I think must be a personal best.

questions.prompt: Do you prefer buying things online or in shops?

segments.text: It depends on what I'm buying. I prefer buying books and electronics online, because it's cheaper and easier.
However, for clothes or shoes I like going to a shop, because I can try them on.
For example, I once bought some shoes online and they were too small, so I had to send them back, which was annoying.
It depends. For books and gadgets, online wins hands down: it's quicker, and there's more choice.
When it comes to clothes, though, I prefer to see and try things on before I part with my money.
I learnt that the hard way after ordering a pair of shoes that were a size too small and having to send them back.

questions.prompt: Where did you spend your last holiday?

segments.text: I spent my last holiday in the south of Italy, near Naples.
We stayed in a small hotel by the sea for a week, with my partner and another couple.
The weather was perfect. We swam every day, and we ate lots of pizza and ice cream. It was one of the best holidays I've ever had.
Last summer we spent a week on the Amalfi coast, which was absolutely stunning.
We rented a little place overlooking the sea, so I woke up to the sound of waves every morning.
Between the swimming, the sightseeing and the pizza, I came home feeling completely recharged.

questions.prompt: What do you like doing when you visit a new place?

segments.text: When I visit a new place, I like walking around without a map.
I think it's the best way to discover small streets and local cafés.
For example, in Lisbon I walked for hours, and I found a little restaurant where I had the best fish of my life. I also like visiting a museum, but only one a day.
The first thing I do is wander aimlessly. You stumble across hidden corners that no guidebook mentions.
I also make a point of eating where the locals eat, rather than in tourist traps.
In Lisbon, that got me the best grilled fish I've ever tasted, in a tiny place with no menu.

questions.prompt: Where would you like to go on your next holiday?

segments.text: I'd really like to visit Japan.
I'm interested in the culture and the food, and I've heard the cities are very clean and safe.
I'm saving money at the moment, and I hope to go in two years. For example, I'd like to see Tokyo and Kyoto, and I'd probably go in spring to see the cherry blossom.
Japan is top of my bucket list. I've been dreaming about it for years: the food, the temples, the mix of old and new.
I've been putting money aside for a while, so with a bit of luck I'll go in two years.
If I had the choice, I'd go in spring for the cherry blossom, even though that's peak season.
